blocks.tk: Magtymguly Pyragy türkmen edebiýatynyň iň meşhur şahyry. Köp alym ony türkmen edebiýatynyň atasy hasaplaýar. Ol 18-nji asyrda, Etrek we Gürgen derýalarynyň arasynda, häzirki Eýranyň Gülüstan welaýatyndaky Hajygowşan obasynda doglupdyr. Onuň doglan ýyly barada çeşmeler dürli: Türkmenistanda 1724-nji ýyl diýýärler, käbir çeşmeler 1733-nji ýyly görkezýär. 2024-nji ýylda onuň 300 ýyllygyny Türkmenistanda we başga ýurtlarda bellediler, UNESKO hem bu senäni sanawyna girizdi.
blocks.en: Magtymguly Pyragy is the best-loved poet of the Turkmen, often called the father of their literature. He was born in the 18th century in Hajji Gowshan, a village between the Etrek and Gürgen rivers in what is now Golestan province in Iran. Sources disagree on the year. Turkmenistan dates his birth to 1724 and marked his 300th anniversary in 2024, an anniversary UNESCO included among those it celebrated in 2024–2025; other sources give about 1733.

blocks.tk: Onuň kakasy Döwletmämmet Azady hem şahyr we mugallym bolupdyr. Magtymguly ilki kakasyndan okapdyr, soňra Buharadaky we Hywadaky medreselerde bilim alypdyr. Onuň okan medreseleriniň biri Buharadaky Gögeldaş medresesidir. Ol ýaşlykda keçe ýasamagy, käbir çeşmelere görä bolsa zergärçiligi hem öwrenipdir. Ol türkmen, pars we arap dillerini bilipdir. Ol obasyndan Meňli atly bir gyzy söýüpdir, ýöne oňa öýlenip bilmändir. Şahyr söýgi goşgularynyň köpüsini Meňlä bagyşlapdyr.
blocks.en: His father, Döwletmämmet Azady, was himself a poet and a teacher. Magtymguly learned first from him, then studied at madrasas in Bukhara, among them the Kukeldash, and in Khiva; he knew Turkmen, Persian and Arabic, and learned felt-making and, some sources say, silversmithing. He took the pen name Pyragy, from an Arabic word for **separated**. As a young man he loved a girl from his village, Meňli, but could not marry her, and many of his love poems are addressed to her.

blocks.tk: Magtymguly goşgularynyň köpüsini dört setirli bentler bilen ýazypdyr. Bu goşgular halk aýdymlaryna meňzeýär, şonuň üçin bagşylar olary dutar bilen aýtmagy gowy görýärler. Şahyryň goşgularynda dünýä, adalat, dostluk we watan barada pikirler köp. Onuň käbir setirleri halk arasynda nakyl ýaly ýaşaýar. Bagşylaryň aýdýan aýdymlarynyň arasynda hem Magtymgulynyň goşgulary köp.
blocks.en: Britannica counts some 800 poems, most of them in the four-line stanzas of Turkmen folk song, with a smaller number of ghazals in the classical style that carry Sufi ideas. Because they sound like folk songs, bagşys sing them to the dutar, and in the 19th century, Britannica notes, his verses spread by word of mouth far beyond the Turkmen, among Kurds, Tajiks and Karakalpaks. His poems speak of the world and its unfairness, of friendship and of the homeland, and some of his lines are quoted like proverbs.

blocks.tk: Magtymgulynyň iň meşhur goşgularynyň biri “Türkmeniň”. Şahyr onda Jeýhun derýasy bilen Hazar deňziniň arasyndaky ýurdy, onuň çöllerini, daglaryny we adamlaryny wasp edýär. Goşgynyň ilkinji iki bendi şeýle:
blocks.en: One of his best-known poems is “Türkmeniň”, “of the Turkmen”. It praises the land between the Jeyhun, the old name of the Amu Darya, and the Caspian Sea: its desert winds, its mountains, its flowers and its people. Here are its first two stanzas, in the modern spelling given on Wikipedia, with our own translation.

blocks.tk: Jeýhun bilen bahry-Hazar arasy, / Çöl üstünden öwser ýeli türkmeniň; / Gül-gunçasy – gara gözüm garasy, / Gara dagdan iner sili türkmeniň.
blocks.en: Between the Jeyhun and the Caspian Sea, / over the desert blows the Turkmen's wind; / its rosebuds are the apple of my eye; / down from the dark mountains come the Turkmen's floods.
blocks.source: Magtymguly Pyragy, “Türkmeniň”, first stanza, 18th century; our translation

blocks.tk: Hak sylamyş bardyr onuň saýasy, / Çyrpynşar çölünde neri, maýasy, / Reňbe-reň gül açar ýaşyl ýaýlasy, / Gark bolmuş reýhana çöli türkmeniň.
blocks.en: Honoured by God, it rests in His shade; / its camels, male and female, frisk across its sands; / flowers of every colour open on its green pastures; / the Turkmen's desert is drowned in sweet basil.
blocks.source: Magtymguly Pyragy, “Türkmeniň”, second stanza, 18th century; our translation

blocks.tk: Magtymguly takmynan 1807-nji ýylda aradan çykypdyr. Onuň mazary Eýranyň Gülüstan welaýatyndaky Aktokaý obasynda. Bu ýere köp adam zyýarata gelýär. Türkmenler ony diňe Türkmenistanda däl, Eýranda hem hormatlaýarlar. Türkmenistanda şahyryň adyny göterýän köçeler, mekdepler, bir şäher we uniwersitet bar, onuň suraty on manatlyk kagyz pulda hem bar.
blocks.en: Magtymguly died around 1807 and is buried at Aq Taqeh, a village in Golestan province, where his tomb is a place of pilgrimage: he is honoured by Turkmen on both sides of the border. In Turkmenistan streets, schools, a town and the state university bear his name, and his portrait is on the 10-manat banknote issued in 2009.

blocks.tk: Şahyryň ýazan goşgularyny häzir hem bagşylar aýdýarlar, okuwçylar bolsa olary mekdepde ýatdan öwrenýärler. Türkmenler oňa diňe şahyr däl, eýsem akyldar hem diýýärler.
blocks.en: Bagşys still sing his poems, and children learn them by heart at school. In Turkmenistan he is spoken of as a thinker, an *akyldar*, as much as a poet.

blocks.title: Reading the Turkmen
blocks.text: Look for this unit's participles: *doglan ýyly* (the year he was born), *şahyryň adyny göterýän köçeler* (streets that bear the poet's name), *şahyryň ýazan goşgulary* (the poems the poet wrote). His life is told in `-(Y)pdYr` (*doglupdyr, okapdyr*), since nobody alive saw it. The poem itself is in an older literary style: *sylamyş* and *bolmuş* are old forms not used in everyday Turkmen today.
